name: Origen of Alexandria
status: Church Father. Not counted a saint.

seo.title: Origen of Alexandria: why he is not a saint, and what he taught
seo.description: Origen in plain words: the boy whose mother hid his clothes, his Bible in six columns, his torture, and why no church counts him a saint.

band.lede: A great Bible scholar of the early Church, tortured for his faith. Some of his ideas were condemned three centuries after he died.

card.line: A great Bible scholar of the early Church, tortured for his faith. Some of his ideas were condemned three centuries after he died.

who: Origen was a teacher and Bible scholar of Alexandria in Egypt. At eighteen he ran its school for new Christians. He learned Hebrew and wrote more than any Christian before him. He was tortured for his faith and died a few years later. Some of his ideas were condemned about three centuries later, and no church counts him a saint.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 185, probably at **Alexandria in Egypt**. His parents were Christians, says Eusebius. The pagan Porphyry said otherwise.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At Alexandria. His father, **Leonides**, taught him the Bible before Greek learning. He made the boy learn and recite passages every day.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: About **253 or 254**, at **Tyre**, today Sour in Lebanon. He was 69.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Tyre. Pilgrims long visited his tomb behind the high altar of the cathedral. Its place is now unknown.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Adamantius**, the “man of adamant”. Eusebius says it was his other name. Jerome says his zeal for the Bible earned it.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: Church Father, in the everyday sense. In strict Catholic usage he is an “ecclesiastical writer”, not a Father.

facts.label: Feast day
facts.text: None. No church keeps one. His father, **St Leonides**, is in the 1916 *Roman Martyrology* on **22 April**. His martyred pupils are there on **28 June**.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: No likeness survives. Western books show an old scholar with books, or a teacher among his students.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: More than any writer before him, says Jerome. Commentaries and sermons on much of the Bible, the Hexapla, *On First Principles*, *Against Celsus* and letters. Most is lost, or survives only in Latin.

portrait.alt: An etching: the bearded Origen sits at a table with a large open book, pointing as he teaches a crowd of young students, while soldiers gather in the street outside the arched windows
portrait.credit: Origen teaching new believers, Jan Luyken, 1700. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Jan Luyken
portrait.caption: An etching by Jan Luyken, 1700. He teaches new believers while soldiers gather outside, as Eusebius tells it. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.

traits.title: prayer and reading, day and night
traits.text: His patron Ambrose wrote that they never ate a meal together without something read aloud. They never went to bed until a brother had read them some Scripture. Jerome, retelling it, says: “Night and day, in fact, were so ordered that prayer only gave place to reading and reading to prayer.”

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 43, to Marcella

traits.title: lived as he taught
traits.text: For years he went barefoot and slept on the ground. He drank no wine and ate only what he needed. He nearly ruined his health. People said “his manner of life was as his doctrine, and his doctrine as his life”.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 3

traits.title: fair to his opponents
traits.text: He answered the pagan Celsus in eight books. Celsus had promised a second book, and Origen asked his patron to send it if it existed. He would refute what was false in it. Or else, he wrote, “laying aside all jealousy, we may testify our approval of whatever truth it may contain”.

cite.text: Against Celsus, Book 8, chapter 76

traits.title: brave, but not reckless
traits.text: As a boy he longed to die a martyr. As a man he did not go looking for death. On Jesus withdrawing after John the Baptist was killed, he wrote: “When a temptation comes which is not in our power to avoid, we must endure it with exceeding nobleness and courage; but, when it is in our power to avoid it, not to do so is rash.”

cite.text: Commentary on Matthew, Book 10, section 23

said.lede: Most of what we know of his life comes from Eusebius, who collected Origen's letters and spoke with people who had known him.

quotes.q: And thus, like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us, a love at once to the Holy Word, the most lovely object of all, Who attracts all irresistibly toward Himself by His unutterable beauty, and to this man, His friend and advocate.
quotes.who: Gregory the Wonderworker, his pupil for five years, in his farewell speech to Origen

cite.text: Oration and Panegyric Addressed to Origen, Argument 6

quotes.q: Origen, whom all but the ignorant acknowledge as the greatest teacher of the Churches next to the Apostles.
quotes.who: Jerome, in 388, before he turned against Origen's ideas

cite.text: Preface to the Book on Hebrew Names

quotes.q: I have praised the commentator but not the theologian, the man of intellect but not the believer, the philosopher but not the apostle.
quotes.who: Jerome, twelve years later, defending himself for having praised Origen

cite.text: Letter 84, section 2

quotes.q: …you may hear again from the labour-loving Origen also.
quotes.who: Athanasius, about 350, defending the Nicene Creed. What Origen wrote “as if inquiring and by way of exercise”, he adds, is not his own view.

cite.text: Defence of the Nicene Definition, chapter 6, section 27

quotes.q: I can not sufficiently express my astonishment, that a man so erudite and well versed in ecclesiastical literature, should not have observed…
quotes.who: Augustine, a critic, on Origen's idea that souls were sent into bodies as a punishment

cite.text: City of God, Book 11, chapter 23

moments.title: The hidden clothes
moments.text: Persecution broke out under the emperor Severus, and Origen's father Leonides was arrested. The boy was set on being a martyr too. His mother begged him to stay. Then she hid all his clothes, so he could not leave the house. So he wrote to his father instead: “Take heed not to change your mind on our account.” Leonides was beheaded. The family's property was seized, and Origen was left with his mother and six younger brothers.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 1 and 2

moments.title: Head of the school at eighteen
moments.text: Persecution had driven the Christian teachers out of the city. So pagans came to the young man to learn the faith. In his eighteenth year he took charge of Alexandria's school for new Christians. He gave up his paid school of grammar. So that he would need no help from others, he sold his valuable books of ancient literature. The buyer paid him four obols a day, and he lived on that for years.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 3

moments.title: Beside the martyrs
moments.text: Several of his first pupils were arrested and killed. He stood by the martyrs in prison, friends and strangers alike, and walked with them to their deaths. He kissed them in public, and the crowds nearly turned on him. Soldiers were posted round the house where he lived. He had to move from house to house.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 3 and 4

moments.title: A deed he was blamed for
moments.text: Eusebius says Origen took Jesus's words about eunuchs too literally (Matthew 19:12) and castrated himself. He taught women as well as men, and he wanted to leave no room for scandal. Eusebius calls it the deed of “an immature and youthful mind”, yet “the highest proof of faith and continence”. His bishop admired it at first. Later he used it against him. Some historians doubt the story. *Britannica* says it “may merely have been hostile gossip”.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 8; Britannica

moments.title: A Bible in six columns
moments.text: He learned Hebrew. Jerome says that was “contrary to the spirit of his time, and of his people”. He hunted down Greek translations of the Old Testament, even some long hidden. One, he said, he found in a jar at Jericho. Then he set them side by side with the Hebrew, column by column. The work is called the Hexapla, for its six columns.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 16; Jerome, Lives, chapter 54

moments.title: Sent for by the emperor's mother
moments.text: His fame reached Mammaea, mother of the emperor Alexander. Eusebius calls her “a most pious woman, if there ever was one”. She was staying at Antioch, and she sent a military escort to bring him to her. He stayed a while and taught her about Christ. Then he hurried back to his work.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 21

moments.title: Ordained, then driven out
moments.text: Sent on church business to Greece, he passed through Palestine. There the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem ordained him a priest. His own bishop, Demetrius, was furious. A council of bishops ordered him out of Alexandria, but let him stay a priest. Then Demetrius and some Egyptian bishops took his priesthood away too. He moved to Caesarea for good.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 23 and 26; Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 118

moments.title: A second school
moments.text: At Caesarea he opened a new school, and pupils came from other countries. The bishops of Jerusalem and Caesarea sat under him “as their only teacher”. Two brothers stayed five years, and both became bishops in Pontus. One of them is remembered as Gregory the Wonderworker.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 27 and 30

words.note: Much of Origen is lost. Some survives in his own Greek. Much survives only in Latin, from Rufinus and Jerome. Rufinus said he left out passages he took for forgeries. Each line says where it comes from.

feature.kicker: After his own bishop condemned him
feature.q: We ought to pity them, not to hate them, to pray for them, not to curse them. For we have been created for blessing, not for cursing.
feature.ctx: From a letter to friends at Alexandria, about the bishops who had cast him out. The Greek is lost. It survives because Jerome translated it, to show that his rival Rufinus had cut it.

cite.text: Letter to friends at Alexandria, quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, section 18

quotes.q: For stronger than all the evils in the soul is the Word, and the healing power that dwells in Him; and this healing He applies, according to the will of God, to every man.
quotes.who: His great hope, written late in life. In the same chapter he leaves open whether evil, once destroyed, could ever arise again.

cite.text: Against Celsus, Book 8, chapter 72

quotes.q: We may therefore make bold to say that the Gospels are the first fruits of all the Scriptures, but that of the Gospels that of John is the first fruits. No one can apprehend the meaning of it except he have lain on Jesus' breast and received from Jesus Mary to be his mother also.
quotes.who: Opening his great commentary on John's Gospel, written for his friend Ambrose.

cite.text: Commentary on John, Book 1, section 6

quotes.q: Be not satisfied with knocking and seeking; for prayer is of all things indispensable to the knowledge of the things of God.
quotes.who: To his former pupil Gregory, on how to read the Bible.

cite.text: Letter to Gregory, section 3

quotes.q: For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars?
quotes.who: On Genesis 1. Some passages, he argues, point past the letter to a hidden meaning.

cite.text: On First Principles, Book 4, chapter 1, section 16

quotes.q: That alone is to be accepted as truth which differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.
quotes.who: The rule he set himself at the start of his boldest book. This part survives only in Rufinus's Latin.

cite.text: On First Principles, Preface, section 2

myths.truth: He rejected it by name, as “the dogma of transmigration, which is foreign to the church of God, and not handed down by the Apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures”. What he did teach, and what was later condemned, is that souls existed before birth. That is a different idea.

cite.text: Commentary on Matthew, Book 13, section 1

myths.claim: Origen said even the devil would be saved.
myths.truth: In a letter he denied it angrily, as “a thing which not even a madman can say”. But Jerome, who read the debate behind the charge, says Origen argued there that the devil fell by his own will, and so could be saved. Augustine, writing in the 420s, believed Origen taught it. So it is still argued.

cite.text: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, sections 18 and 19; City of God, Book 21, chapter 17

myths.truth: Rufinus said a bishop hostile to Origen claimed to have read 6,000 of his books. Jerome called the story false. Eusebius's list of Origen's works, he said, came to “not a third of that number of books”.

cite.text: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, section 22

myths.claim: He was condemned as a heretic in his own lifetime.
myths.truth: Not for his teaching, Jerome says. His bishop had him banished and deposed after the ordination. The censure, Jerome writes, was not “because of the novelty or heterodoxy of his doctrines”. It was because men “could not tolerate” his eloquence. Jerome wrote that about 384, before he turned against Origen. *Britannica* adds that his bishop was also shocked by his view that even the devil could repent. Councils condemned his ideas only after his death.

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 33, to Paula, section 4; Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 118; Britannica

myths.claim: He read the whole Bible as allegory, and did not believe its history.
myths.truth: He said the opposite: “the passages that are true in their historical meaning are much more numerous than those which are interspersed with a purely spiritual signification”. He did think some passages could not be literal, such as days before there was a sun.

cite.text: On First Principles, Book 4, chapter 1, section 19

myths.claim: Gregory of Nazianzus called Origen the whetstone of us all.
myths.truth: The 1911 *Catholic Encyclopedia* gives no work of Gregory's for it. Its source is the Suda, a Byzantine lexicon of about 1000. What is certain is that Gregory and Basil the Great made the Philocalia, a book of passages from Origen. About Easter 382 Gregory sent a copy to a friend, “containing a selection of passages useful to students of literature”.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, 1911; Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 115

stood.lede: Most of these lines are his own words. Two come to us through others: Eusebius, and Jerome, who quoted Origen to attack him. His hope that the Word will win every soul is close to the teaching later condemned.

lie.work: Miscellanies, Book 6 (lost), as Jerome quotes it in Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 18

calling.work: Letter to his father, as Eusebius records it in Church History, Book 6, chapter 2

circle.name: Leonides
circle.text: His father. He taught Origen the Bible and was beheaded for the faith in 202. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* counts him a saint.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 1 and 2

circle.name: Clement of Alexandria
circle.text: Eusebius says Origen studied under him as a boy. Photius says Origen followed him as head of the school.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 6; Photius, codex 118

circle.name: Demetrius of Alexandria
circle.text: His bishop. He put Origen in charge of the school, then turned on him after the ordination. Jerome says he “wrote everywhere to injure his reputation”. The Coptic Church honours Demetrius as a saint.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives, chapter 54; Coptic Synaxarium, 12 Baba

circle.name: Heraclas
circle.text: An early pupil, then his assistant. He took over the school and later became bishop of Alexandria. *Britannica* says he ended by refusing communion with Origen. The 1911 *Catholic Encyclopedia* says there is no proof he broke with him.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 3, 15 and 26; Britannica; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1911

circle.name: Ambrose, his patron
circle.text: Not Ambrose of Milan. A rich man whom Origen won over from the Valentinian sect. He paid for Origen's secretaries and kept him writing.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapters 18 and 23

circle.name: Gregory the Wonderworker
circle.text: His pupil at Caesarea for five years. His farewell speech to Origen survives, and so does Origen's letter to him.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 30

circle.name: Julius Africanus
circle.text: A friendly critic. He argued that the story of Susanna in Daniel was a later forgery. Origen sent a long, courteous reply.

cite.text: The letters of Africanus and Origen

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: He praised Origen and translated his sermons. Then he turned against his ideas, and fell out bitterly with Rufinus over them.

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 84; Britannica

circle.name: Rufinus
circle.text: He put *On First Principles* into Latin. He said he left out passages that clashed with the faith, taking them for forgeries by others. Much of Origen survives only in his Latin.

cite.text: Rufinus, preface to On First Principles, Book 3; Britannica

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: Writing in the 420s, he judged the Church right to condemn Origen's hope that even the devil would be freed.

cite.text: City of God, Book 21, chapter 17

circle.name: Basil the Great
circle.text: With his friend Gregory of Nazianzus, he made the Philocalia, a book of passages from Origen.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 115; Britannica

circle.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
circle.text: He made the Philocalia with Basil, and sent a copy to a friend as a gift.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 115

death.big: He died at Tyre about 253 or 254, at the age of 69. A few years before, he had been tortured for his faith.
paras: In 250 the emperor Decius began a persecution. Origen was chained and thrown into a dungeon, with an iron collar round his neck. For many days his feet were stretched wide in the stocks. He was threatened with fire.
Eusebius says his judge “strove eagerly with all his might not to end his life”. Origen survived. The letters he wrote afterwards were “full of comfort to those needing aid”.
He died a few years later at Tyre, when Gallus was emperor, and was buried there. No last words are recorded.

later.title: Another account
later.text: Photius, writing in the 800s, read a defence of Origen by the martyr Pamphilus. Pamphilus and others said Origen “quitted this life by a glorious martyrdom at Caesarea” under Decius. Photius thought the Tyre account truer, “unless the letters supposed to have been written by him after the Decian persecution are spurious”.

cite.text: Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 118

saint.big: No. No church counts him a saint. His father and several of his pupils are saints. He is not.

churches.note: The OCA: his teaching on souls condemned in 553
It honours the bishop who excommunicated him
Not in Common Worship or Lesser Feasts and Fasts
Not in the Missouri Synod's list

paras: Many saints admired him. Even the 1909 *Catholic Encyclopedia* says his works fell under the Church's ban “though their author lived the life of a saint”.

Methodius, a bishop martyred in 311, wrote against him. From the 390s a bitter quarrel broke out over his ideas. In the 540s and 550s, under the emperor Justinian, two ideas linked to him were condemned. One was that souls exist before they are born. The other was that all things, even demons, will at last be restored. The Fifth Council, in 553, names him among heretics.

How much of this he taught is still argued. Much of his work survives only in a smoothed Latin translation, or in his enemies' quotations. *Britannica* warns that his opponents “were not above misquoting Origen and ascribing to him the words of later Origenists”.

Pope Benedict XVI still gave two talks praising him in 2007. The Episcopal Church keeps no day for him. But its calendar, in Clement's entry, calls him “the most eminent theologian of early Greek Christianity”.

quotes.q: If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches and Origen, as well as their impious writings…
quotes.who: The Fifth Council, Constantinople, 553. Some scholars thought his name was added later.

cite.text: The Fifth Council, anathema 11

quotes.q: If anyone asserts the fabulous pre-existence of souls, and shall assert the monstrous restoration which follows from it: let him be anathema.
quotes.who: The first of fifteen anathemas against Origen's teaching. They may come from a synod held before the council.

cite.text: The fifteen anathemas, anathema 1

quotes.q: But the Church, not without reason, condemned him for this and other errors.
quotes.who: Augustine, on the hope that even the devil and his angels would be freed

cite.text: City of God, Book 21, chapter 17

quotes.q: Were Origen and Origenism anathematized? Many learned writers believe so; an equal number deny that they were condemned; most modern authorities are either undecided or reply with reservations.
quotes.who: The *Catholic Encyclopedia*, 1911, on whether the council itself condemned him

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), Origen and Origenism

tidbits.text: As a boy he puzzled his father with questions about the deeper meaning of Scripture. The story went that his father would stand over the sleeping boy, bare his chest and kiss it, as if the Spirit of God lived there.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 2

tidbits.text: Jerome said that in his other books Origen outdid every other writer. In his ten volumes on the Song of Songs, he outdid himself.

cite.text: Jerome, Preface to Origen's Homilies on the Song of Songs

tidbits.text: He had his pupils read every philosopher and poet of old, rejecting nothing. Only the atheists, who deny that there is a God or a providence, were not worth reading, he held.

cite.text: Gregory the Wonderworker, Oration and Panegyric Addressed to Origen, Argument 13
